passage_text: Researchers at a university investigated the effect of caffeine on short-term memory retention among college students. A total of 120 participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: caffeine (n=40), placebo (n=40), and no caffeine (n=40). All participants underwent a standardized memory test consisting of 50 word pairs presented visually. After a 30‑minute break, recall performance was measured. The mean recall scores (out of 100; 2 points per word pair) for each group were recorded. The study aimed to determine whether caffeine ingestion prior to the test would enhance memory retention compared to a placebo or no caffeine condition. Results suggested a graded effect, with the caffeine group outperforming the placebo group, which in turn outperformed the no‑caffeine group. The authors discussed potential mechanisms such as increased arousal and neurotransmitter modulation, while noting limitations including a homogeneous sample and short follow‑up period. They concluded that moderate caffeine intake may transiently improve memory recall in young adults, but further research is needed to assess long‑term effects and applicability to other populations.

stem: Calculate the mean difference in recall scores between the caffeine and no‑caffeine groups.
explanation: Correct: A) 78 (caffeine) − 68 (no caffeine) = 10. Why the others are wrong: B) 6 is caffeine minus placebo (78 − 72). C) 4 is placebo minus no caffeine (72 − 68). D) 12 does not equal any difference between the group means.
trap: Subtracting the placebo mean (72) instead of the no-caffeine mean (68), which gives 6 points rather than 10.
